column3: It directly repeats the final setting where fatigue does not touch its people and adds that they are not expelled from it.
Its explicit denial of languor gives a close parallel to the focus's denial that fatigue can touch within the settled abode.
It supplies only the general pattern of harm touching people, against which the focus states protective non-contact.
The call to the abode of peace closely clarifies the focus's divinely granted, secure permanent dwelling.
The immediately preceding ayah identifies the garden residents whose settled abode is described in the focus.
A lasting punishment that settles upon its recipient provides a clear adverse counterpart to the focus's gracious settled abode.
The Fire as an abode of permanence supplies a boundary contrast to the protected permanent dwelling in the focus.
The immediately preceding removal of sorrow completes the focus's picture of a residence free from exhausting affliction.
Job's fatigue and suffering are described as touching him, making the focus's prevention of such contact more concrete.
It treats fatigue endured in God's path as recorded good, contrasting earthly exertion with the focus's fatigue-free abode.
Its command not to grieve or remain in constriction offers only a limited emotional parallel to the focus's complete relief.
Its request concerning remaining disbelievers does not clarify the focus's permanent abode or freedom from fatigue.
It sharply contrasts the gracious settling in the focus with leaders settling their people in an abode of ruin.
The unchanging divine pattern gives only a broad contextual parallel to the stability of the focus's settled abode.
It directly presents the later abode as better and as the excellent dwelling for the God-fearing.
The abode of peace closely parallels the focus's protected residence, though this similar destination is already established earlier.

Its warning about respite increasing sin does not add to the focus's abode or relief from fatigue.

Divine bounty and freedom from fear or grief offer a partial benefit parallel, without the focus's settled-abode language.

Its rules for written debts do not add to the focus's permanent abode or relief from fatigue.

The temporary standing-place in a transport claim does not clarify the focus's permanent dwelling.

Its marriage and justice regulation does not clarify the focus's final residence.
The prohibition on harmful touching and its punishment forms only a limited contrast to the focus's protected non-contact.

Its test and warning scene does not add to the focus's protected residence.

Freedom from idle and false speech adds a limited parallel of a purified final environment.

The House as a place of return and safety offers an indirect spatial parallel to a secure abode.
Its absence of idle and sinful speech gives only a secondary parallel of protected final life.
The believers' response to the confederates does not clarify the focus's abode or freedom from fatigue.
Old age touching Abraham supplies a limited bodily-contact contrast to the focus's prevention of fatigue.

Individual responsibility and return to God do not clarify the focus's permanent dwelling.

The demand for the promised time does not clarify the focus's protected residence.
People left motionless in their dwelling provide a limited adverse image of an abode after judgment.

It gives entry into gardens with rivers and abiding therein as the reward of obedience.

It places the God-fearing in gardens and springs, supplying the setting completed by the focus's freedom from fatigue.
The removal of rancor and brotherly repose in the garden directly strengthens the focus's picture of complete protected relief.
It promises gardens of Eden with rivers for believers who do righteous deeds.
It identifies the gardens of Firdaws as the lasting hospitality for faith and righteous action.
Its statement of abiding forever in Firdaws directly reinforces permanent residence.
It promises entry into the Garden for those who repent, believe, and act rightly.
The gardens of Eden promised by the Merciful directly parallel a divinely granted permanent dwelling.
The warning that expulsion from the garden would bring hardship forms a clear contrast to the focus's secure fatigue-free residence.
It presents entry into gardens with rivers and adornment, continuing the resident scene found near the focus.
The inheritors of Firdaws abiding therein provide a direct parallel of a permanent final residence.

It gives gardens of refuge as a prepared recompense for faith and righteous deeds.
It supplies a scene of Garden residents joyfully occupied, extending the focus's final-abode condition.
It identifies gardens of bliss as the setting of the honored servants.
The groups led into the Garden receive a greeting of peace and are told to enter it abiding forever.
It asks that believers and their righteous families enter the gardens of Eden that God promised them.
It begins the assurance to the steadfast that they need not fear or grieve, a close emotional parallel to the focus's complete relief.
It promises believers the Garden and whatever they desire there, directly supporting the focus's protected final dwelling.

It commands entry into the Garden in joy, supplying the destination and affective condition of the focus's residents.

Its exclusion of death after the first death adds another form of final security to the focus's permanent residence.

It places the God-fearing in gardens and bliss, supplying the broader final setting of the focus.

It promises believers gardens with rivers and eternal abiding, accompanied by divine good news.
It calls toward a garden as wide as the heavens and earth, prepared for believers in God and His messengers.
It directly promises forgiveness, gardens with rivers, and good dwellings in gardens of Eden.
It states that faith brings entry into gardens with rivers and lasting residence.
It combines belief, righteous action, gardens with rivers, eternal abiding, and divine provision.
